title: Build a Twelve-Month Money Plan
meta_description: Turn the next twelve months into a dated financial plan for cash flow, reserves, debt, taxes, retirement, insurance, credit and family records.

sections.heading: Move 1: Put the Year on One Cash Calendar
paragraphs: A twelve-month money plan should begin with dates, not resolutions. The opening photograph shows cash, receipts, a calculator and an open planner because each goal competes with obligations that arrive on a schedule. List paydays, benefit deposits, tax dates, insurance renewals, tuition, travel, annual subscriptions, property charges and known medical costs. A yearly view exposes clusters that a typical monthly budget hides.

Build the calendar from statements and contracts rather than memory. Mark the due date, expected amount, account used and whether the charge can change. Convert predictable annual costs into monthly sinking-fund transfers. A $1,200 premium due in six months is not a surprise; it is a $200 monthly funding problem. Keep an uncertainty range for bills that depend on usage, assessment or renewal pricing.

Then map income reliability. Salary may be stable while bonuses, commissions, overtime, contract work and tax refunds are not. Fund required costs from dependable income where possible. Assign uncertain income only after it arrives. If pay is irregular, establish a conservative monthly base, hold stronger-month surplus in a smoothing account and avoid building fixed commitments around the best month.

The [[S1|CFPB financial-empowerment toolkit]] emphasizes cash-flow timing because a household can have enough income for the month and still lack cash when a bill is due. Review the next eight weeks every payday and the full twelve months once a month. The plan remains annual, but decisions happen at shorter intervals.

Finish this move with three numbers: required monthly floor, known irregular costs over the next year and minimum checking buffer. Those figures anchor every later move. Without them, a savings transfer, debt payment or investment increase can look affordable while quietly colliding with a bill.

Add decision windows, not just due dates. A renewal due June 1 may require quotes in April; a tuition bill may require aid forms months earlier; a property-tax appeal may have a filing deadline before payment. Mark the first action date, final decision date and cash date separately. This prevents a funded obligation from becoming expensive because the household missed the point when it could compare, cancel or change course.

Keep one change log beside the calendar. When a premium, due date, payroll deduction or transfer changes, record the old value, new value, effective date and reason. This prevents different spreadsheets and automatic instructions from drifting apart. Reconcile the calendar with actual account activity after the first month, then correct timing assumptions. If the account repeatedly needs rescue from another account, the buffer or bill date is wrong even when the annual arithmetic balances. Ask providers whether a due date can be moved to reduce clustering, but confirm the effective cycle and any transitional payment before relying on it. The calendar should describe how money truly moves, not how the household wishes it moved.

sections.heading: Move 2: Give Each Goal a Date and Funding Line
paragraphs: “Save more” is not a fundable instruction. Name the purchase or protection, target amount, deadline and account. Separate short goals such as travel or a deductible from long goals such as retirement. Calculate the contribution required from now to the date, then test whether that amount fits after required bills and minimum debt payments. If it does not, change the amount, date or design before relying on hope.

Rank goals by consequence, not excitement. Housing continuity, essential transportation, health, taxes and minimum obligations usually outrank discretionary upgrades. A goal can still matter without being funded first. Place each goal in one of four states: active contribution, maintenance, waiting for capacity or rejected. This prevents twelve simultaneous priorities from receiving token transfers that complete none.

Use separate ledger labels even when money sits in one insured account. “Emergency,” “car insurance,” “holiday travel” and “home repair” are not interchangeable merely because the bank balance is combined. A sinking fund serves a known future expense; an emergency reserve covers uncertainty. Spending the annual-premium balance on an emergency creates another predictable emergency later.

Define completion and maintenance. After a deductible fund reaches its target, redirect the contribution rather than letting it vanish into ordinary spending. If inflation or a changed quote raises the target, revise the funding line. Keep automatic transfers visible in the plan; automation is execution, not proof that the chosen amount remains right.

Every quarter, ask whether the goal still deserves its place. Circumstances can make a once-important purchase unnecessary or bring a new obligation forward. Reallocation is not failure when the decision is explicit and recorded.

For joint households, identify whether a goal is shared or individual and who can authorize a transfer. Agreement on the label does not guarantee agreement on the trade-off. Write what pauses the contribution: job loss, reserve falling below its floor, an insurance increase or another stated trigger. A pause rule protects higher priorities without forcing the household to renegotiate the entire plan during stress.

sections.heading: Move 3: Build the Emergency Floor Before the Perfect Fund
paragraphs: Emergency savings should be sized from household risk, not one universal number. Begin with a starter floor capable of absorbing a likely urgent cost without high-interest borrowing. Then build an income-replacement layer from essential monthly burn, income stability, replacement time, dependants, insurance deductibles and plausible property or vehicle failures. A stable dual-income household and a single variable-income household do not need identical reserves.

Keep this money accessible and protected from market volatility. Verify whether the bank or credit union and ownership category provide applicable federal insurance. The reserve can earn interest, but yield is secondary to principal stability, liquidity and operational access. Test the withdrawal route before an emergency and maintain a second payment method in case an account is frozen or a card is compromised.

Define permitted uses in writing: essential expense during income interruption, urgent health need, required deductible, safety repair or another named event. A sale item, routine annual bill or predictable holiday is not an emergency. Clear rules reduce negotiation at the moment of stress and make replenishment expectations visible.

Use the [[S2|CFPB research on emergency savings]] as evidence that cash resilience and financial hardship are connected, not as a universal target. Your amount must come from the risk inventory. Stress-test one month without the highest earner’s income, one major deductible and one essential repair. The reserve should not require all three to occur separately.

Schedule a six-month reserve review and an immediate review after job, housing, family or insurance changes. When the fund is used correctly, celebrate that it performed its job, then activate the replenishment line before restoring lower-priority contributions.

Keep the reserve separate from money already promised to taxes, deposits or bills. A large bank balance can create false confidence when most of it has a near-term owner. Calculate “unassigned emergency cash” after subtracting those commitments. If the household receives a windfall, restore depleted reserves and known obligations before raising the lifestyle baseline. Temporary cash should not automatically create permanent monthly spending.

sections.heading: Move 4: Audit Insurance Against the Losses You Cannot Carry
paragraphs: Collect declarations pages and policy summaries for health, auto, home or renters, flood where relevant, disability, liability and life coverage. Record insurer, renewal date, premium, limit, deductible, major exclusions and agent or claim contact. The purpose is not to buy every policy. It is to identify losses that would overwhelm savings, income or family obligations and confirm which contract is meant to respond.

The [[S8|NAIC recommends periodic policy review]], particularly after marriage, divorce, birth, new employment, a mortgage or other life changes. Compare coverage on the same limits rather than shopping from premium alone. A cheaper quote can reflect a larger deductible, narrower property valuation, removed endorsement or lower liability limit. Ask questions in writing and retain answers with the policy.

Coordinate deductibles with the emergency floor. A high deductible can lower premium but transfers more of the loss back to the household. It works only when that cash exists and the policy still handles catastrophic severity. Review replacement-cost assumptions, valuable-item limits, drivers, mileage, occupancy, home business, rental use and excluded hazards. Incorrect facts can matter at claim time.

For life and disability protection, estimate the obligation rather than choosing a round benefit. Consider income replacement, debt, childcare, caregiving, education and available assets. Benefits at work may be useful but can change with employment. Confirm ownership, portability, waiting period, benefit definition and beneficiary records.
Put renewal reminders on the cash calendar at least a month before expiration. That creates time to compare, correct and fund instead of accepting an automatic increase because the deadline arrived.

Record claim procedures before a loss. Know the notice channel, emergency mitigation duties, inventory evidence and deadline language in the contract. Store carrier contacts outside the insured property and photograph relevant conditions without waiting for a disaster. For health coverage, review network, prescription and out-of-pocket rules during the applicable enrollment window. Coverage that exists on paper can still be hard to use when records and contacts are missing.

sections.heading: Move 5: Check Withholding Before the Final Paychecks
paragraphs: Tax withholding is a payment system, not a score. Compare year-to-date wages, withholding, other income, deductions and credits with the expected full-year picture. A new job, multiple jobs, self-employment, marriage, divorce, dependant change, investment gain or retirement distribution can alter the result. Waiting until filing season converts a planning question into a refund or balance due.

The [[S4|IRS Publication 505]] and Tax Withholding Estimator can help employees assess whether federal withholding should increase or decrease. Use current official tools and the household’s actual pay information. State and local obligations require their own review. Self-employed and other taxpayers without sufficient withholding may need estimated payments under applicable rules.

Choose a manageable outcome. Some households prefer a cushion against an amount due; others value more cash in each paycheck. The objective is neither the biggest refund nor a zero result at any cost. It is timely payment that avoids penalties and a filing outcome the household can absorb. Keep a separate tax reserve for income on which no tax is withheld.

Review any proposed tax move for economics before tax effects. Spending $1 solely to claim a deduction does not ordinarily create $1 of tax savings. Retirement, health and charitable decisions can have tax consequences, but the underlying goal and eligibility come first. Preserve receipts, basis records and confirmation documents throughout the year rather than rebuilding them at filing.
Schedule the first review after a few representative pay periods and another early enough to change remaining payments. Recheck immediately after a significant income or household change.

Reconcile the plan with filing readiness. Confirm names, taxpayer identification details, account routing for payments or refunds and access to prior returns. Track expected information forms and follow up when one is missing rather than filing from an incomplete guess. If the household made a significant sale, exercised compensation, moved states or started a business, schedule qualified advice early enough for an action to remain available.

sections.heading: Move 6: Raise Retirement Saving Without Breaking Cash Flow
paragraphs: Review every workplace plan and individual retirement account: contribution rate, employer formula, vesting, investment selection, fees, beneficiaries and whether old accounts remain scattered. Confirm the current official contribution rules before changing payroll. Limits and eligibility can change, and contributions across certain plans may interact. Do not use an old article’s number as the authority for a current election.

Capture an available employer match only after understanding the formula and vesting. Then test a modest contribution increase against the cash calendar. A one-percentage-point rise can be easier to absorb after a raise or debt payoff than a dramatic January target. If high-cost revolving debt or an absent emergency floor would force immediate borrowing, coordinate the goals rather than maximizing one account in isolation.

Review underlying investments, not just account balance. Allocation should match time horizon, risk capacity and other household assets. Employer stock can create concentration because job income and investment value may weaken together. Use broad diversification deliberately and understand the target-date fund’s allocation, glide path and fees if it is the default.

Investor.gov advises investors to review allocation, rebalancing needs and fees periodically. Rebalancing restores intended risk; it does not predict next year’s winner. Contributions can often direct new money toward underweighted assets without taxable sales. Consider taxes and transaction costs before changing holdings.
Document the next increase trigger—raise, loan payoff, benefit change or a calendar date—and name who will execute it. A plan without a trigger tends to wait for a month that never feels inexpensive.

Check the employment transition plan even when no move is expected. Note the plan administrator, loan balance, vesting date and distribution choices. A sudden departure can compress the decision period and invite an expensive cash-out or rushed rollover. Compare leaving assets, a new employer plan and an IRA on investment options, fees, services and legal protections. Do not move money merely because a salesperson made the paperwork easy.

sections.heading: Move 7: Turn Every Debt Into a Payoff Decision
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows a card, laptop, cash and calculator because debt reduction must connect the account to the household’s real cash. Build one inventory containing creditor, balance, annual percentage rate, minimum, due date, remaining term, collateral, promotional-rate end and prepayment rules. Reconcile the list with statements and credit reports; memory often omits a fee, small balance or deferred-interest condition.

Keep all required payments current, then select where extra money goes. The [[S3|CFPB debt action plan]] describes two common approaches: highest interest first can reduce costly interest, while smallest balance first can create faster visible progress. The best execution method is the one the household can sustain, but the cost difference should be visible before choosing.

Protect a starter reserve while paying aggressively. Sending every dollar to debt can create a cycle in which the next repair returns to the card. For secured or protected federal obligations, understand consequences and options before accelerating. A lower rate, consolidation or refinance can help only after fees, lost protections, new term and total cost are compared.

Set a specific extra payment, source and date. When one balance closes, redirect its old payment to the next target or another stated priority. Confirm the account’s final payoff and monitor for trailing interest or recurring charges. Decide separately whether to close an unused revolving account based on fee, fraud monitoring, spending control and credit implications.
Measure progress with principal retired, interest avoided and monthly obligation released—not merely a lower payment created by extending the term.

Create contingency instructions for a reduced-income month. State which extra payment stops first, which creditor should be contacted and which benefits or hardship channels are legitimate. Do not wait for delinquency to learn how a servicer accepts requests. Preserve agreements and confirmation numbers. A payoff plan is stronger when it can slow safely; otherwise one missed commission or medical leave can destroy an aggressive schedule and force new borrowing.

sections.heading: Move 8: Read All Three Credit Reports and Secure Access
paragraphs: Obtain reports through the federally authorized source and review identity details, accounts, balances, payment status and inquiries. A credit score is a model output; the report is the underlying file. The [[S6|CFPB recommends regular report review]] to identify errors and potential identity theft. Checking your own report does not function like applying for new credit.

Create a dispute packet for any error: report identifier, exact item, explanation and supporting copies. Send it through the appropriate reporting company and furnisher process, preserve proof and track deadlines. Do not dispute accurate information merely because it is unfavorable, and do not pay a credit-repair seller for a secret deletion method.

Strengthen account access at the same time. Use unique passwords, multifactor authentication, updated recovery details and transaction alerts. Remove old phone numbers and email addresses. Inventory who has authorized-user access and which third-party apps can see account data. Freeze or alert files when appropriate for the threat and household borrowing plans.

Review credit before a mortgage, rental, auto loan or job process leaves little correction time. Space applications deliberately and compare complete offers. A small score movement matters less than avoiding an expensive product, inaccurate file or unaffordable payment.
Put the next report review on the calendar. Security is not a one-day cleanup; it is an access system with named recovery steps if a device or identity credential is lost.

If a freeze is used, document how each household member can manage it without storing personal identification numbers insecurely. A freeze can reduce certain new-account fraud but does not prevent misuse of existing accounts, tax identity fraud or every scam. Continue statement monitoring and protect government and tax credentials. Security works in layers: report controls, account alerts, device access, careful verification and a recovery procedure.

sections.heading: Move 9: Reprice Recurring Bills and Cancel Quiet Leakage
paragraphs: Export three months of bank and card transactions and identify every recurring charge. Label each as essential contract, valued subscription, duplicate, unused, price-increased or unknown. Annual renewals require a full-year statement review because they may not appear in a short sample. Search email for renewal confirmations and inspect app-store billing separately.

For valued services, compare the current plan with actual use. Renegotiate internet, phone, insurance and memberships where switching costs justify the work. Do not cancel protection or essential service merely to produce an impressive savings total. Confirm termination date, refund, equipment return and loss of bundled discounts in writing.

Redirect savings immediately. A canceled $25 charge does not improve a goal if $25 dissolves into unrelated spending. Add it to the emergency, debt or investment transfer on the same day. Keep a cancellation ledger with the old amount, effective date and destination. Verify one later statement to ensure billing stopped.

Also inspect bank fees, investment expenses and loan add-ons. Small ongoing costs compound across years. Investor.gov notes that fees reduce investment results, even when they appear modest. Compare cost with the service received rather than assuming either the cheapest or most complex product is best.
Repeat a light subscription scan each quarter and a contract review before renewals. The purpose is not endless negotiation; it is preventing silent decisions from renewing indefinitely.

Audit convenience costs without pretending all convenience is waste. Delivery, software or professional help can buy time and reliability that support work or caregiving. Keep services whose value exceeds their full cost and remove those renewed by inertia. For each retained charge, write the use case and next review date. This turns the exercise from indiscriminate austerity into a recurring allocation decision.

sections.heading: Move 10: Rebalance Investments Around the Actual Deadline
paragraphs: List every investment account, goal, withdrawal date and target allocation. Household allocation includes old employer plans, IRAs, taxable accounts, education accounts and concentrated shares—not just the brokerage screen used most often. Calculate exposures across accounts so overlapping funds and employer stock are visible.

Compare current allocation with the written target and risk capacity. A market rise can make a portfolio riskier without any new purchase. Rebalance using contributions, distributions or trades while considering taxes and fees. Do not sell solely because an asset rose or buy solely because another fell; each trade should move the portfolio toward the plan.

Bring near-term money out of dependence on a favorable market date. Tuition, a down payment or required distribution due soon needs a stability plan. Long-horizon retirement money can usually tolerate more volatility, but only if the household will not panic-sell or need it for an uncovered emergency.

Check fund expense ratios, advisory fees, commissions and cash drag. Compare performance with an appropriate benchmark after costs and across a suitable period; a strong recent return does not prove skill. Verify professional registration and understand how advice is paid for.
Write a rebalancing rule—calendar review, allocation band or both—and avoid unplanned changes between reviews unless the goal or household facts genuinely change.

Review account purpose before performance. An account may lag an equity benchmark because it deliberately holds bonds or cash for a nearer liability. That is not automatically a defect. Conversely, a strong return can conceal excessive concentration. Evaluate whether the portfolio took the intended risk and remains capable of funding the goal. Benchmark choice, after-fee return and downside behavior belong together in the review.

sections.heading: Move 11: Build the Financial Emergency File
paragraphs: Create a secure inventory of identification, bank and retirement accounts, loans, insurance policies, income sources, tax records, property documents, medical information and key contacts. Record where originals are stored and how an authorized person can gain access. Do not put full passwords or sensitive numbers into an unprotected spreadsheet merely because the file is convenient.

FEMA’s [[S7|Emergency Financial First Aid Kit]] organizes household, financial, legal, medical and contact records for recovery. Use encrypted digital storage with tested recovery and a protected physical copy where appropriate. A disaster can remove power, phone access and the home containing the only file, so avoid a single point of failure.

Add a household property inventory with dated photographs, model and serial numbers, receipts for major items and appraisals where relevant. This can support insurance discussions and claims. Update after major purchases, renovations or disposal. Confirm that another trusted adult knows the carrier names, contacts and file location.

Include an action sheet for lost wallet, stolen identity, death, disability, disaster and account compromise. List verified phone numbers obtained independently, not links copied from an alarming message. Name which bills remain automatic and which require manual action if the main earner cannot manage them.
Test retrieval once a year. A complete file that nobody can unlock is not preparedness; an accessible file without safeguards is an identity risk. The design must satisfy both continuity and privacy.

Minimize sensitive data while preserving usefulness. The file may list an institution and last four digits rather than a complete account number, with access instructions stored separately. Record document expiration and review dates so passports, directives or contact details do not silently age. If cloud storage is used, test access from a replacement device and decide how multifactor authentication works when the primary phone is unavailable.

sections.heading: Move 12: Update Beneficiaries, Authority and the Handoff
paragraphs: The late photograph shows a couple signing formal documents because the final move converts intentions into valid instructions. Review beneficiaries on retirement accounts, life insurance and transfer-on-death arrangements. These designations may control assets independently of a will. Confirm primary and contingent beneficiaries, percentages, legal names and contact information after birth, death, marriage, divorce or another household change.

Review wills, trusts where appropriate, powers of attorney, health directives, guardianship choices and property titles with qualified local professionals. Requirements vary by state and document. Do not treat an online template as executed merely because fields are complete. Signing, witnessing, notarization, storage and later amendments can determine whether instructions work.

Map the operational handoff. Who can pay bills during incapacity? Who knows about digital assets, subscriptions, business obligations, pets, dependants and safe-deposit access? Give the responsible people enough information to locate documents without broadcasting sensitive details. Confirm that an executor, agent or guardian is willing to serve.

The NAIC advises policyholders to revisit beneficiaries and coverage as family circumstances change. A will does not automatically rewrite every insurance designation. Coordinate the documents rather than updating one and assuming the rest follow. Ask legal and tax professionals about conflicts or unintended consequences.

Close the annual plan with a one-page dashboard: current cash floor, reserve target, debt focus, saving rate, insurance review date, tax checkpoint, allocation, document location and next quarterly meeting. Assign each action to a person and date. The plan is finished only when the calendar, transfers, forms and records can execute it.

Run a tabletop exercise: imagine the primary financial manager is unavailable for thirty days. Ask another authorized adult to locate the dashboard, identify the next bills, find policies and explain whom to call without moving real money. Record each failure and repair the system. This practical test reveals missing authority, inaccessible passwords and undocumented routines more reliably than reading the binder from the perspective of the person who created it.

Schedule the next annual reset before closing the file. Preserve the current dashboard, twelve-month cash history, reserve withdrawals, debt progress, policy changes, tax result and investment allocation as the starting evidence. At the next review, compare forecasts with outcomes: which irregular costs were missed, which transfer failed, which risk changed and which goal no longer mattered. Carry forward only actions that remain relevant. A twelve-month plan is not a permanent personal-finance constitution; it is a controlled operating cycle. Archive proof of completed actions separately from pending work so nobody mistakes an intention for an executed change. Its strongest feature is that every year begins with better records, clearer ownership and fewer hidden assumptions than the year before.

summary: Build the year on one cash calendar containing income dates, required bills, renewals, tax checkpoints and known irregular costs. Review the next eight weeks every payday. Mark the first action date as well as the final payment deadline.

Convert predictable annual obligations into monthly sinking-fund transfers. They are timing problems, not emergencies, and should not consume the emergency reserve. Write the event that pauses each goal so higher priorities remain protected.

Give each goal an amount, deadline, account and contribution. If the contribution does not fit, revise the amount, date or design before relying on uncertain income. Subtract already-committed cash before calling a bank balance an emergency reserve.

Rank goals by consequence and place each in an explicit state: active, maintenance, waiting for capacity or rejected. Do not pretend every goal is first priority. Keep claim contacts and evidence outside the property or device they protect.

Build emergency cash in layers: a starter floor and an income-replacement reserve sized from essential burn, employment risk, dependants, deductibles and plausible repairs. Collect expected tax forms and investigate missing information before filing a return.

Review insurance by matching severe losses with coverage, limits, deductibles and exclusions. Compare equal coverage and update facts after life, work, property or household changes. Document rollover choices before a sudden job departure compresses the decision period.

Check federal withholding and estimated-payment needs before the final pay periods. Use current official tools and repeat the review after material income or family changes. Create reduced-income instructions so an aggressive payoff schedule can slow safely.

Review retirement contributions, employer matching, vesting, beneficiaries, investment allocation and fees. Increase saving through a dated trigger that the cash calendar can support. Combine report controls with existing-account alerts, device security and recovery procedures.

Inventory every debt, keep required payments current and choose an extra-payment method deliberately. Redirect each retired payment instead of allowing it to disappear. Keep useful convenience deliberately; cancel recurring services that survive only through inertia.

Review credit reports for identity data, unfamiliar accounts, incorrect balances and payment status. Preserve dispute evidence and strengthen passwords, recovery details and alerts. Judge investments against their actual goal and intended risk, not an unsuitable benchmark.

Audit subscriptions, contracts, banking fees and investment expenses. Redirect verified savings to a named goal on the same day a recurring charge is removed. Minimize exposed sensitive data and test emergency-file access from a replacement device.

Calculate investment exposure across every account, compare it with the target allocation and rebalance under a written rule while considering taxes, fees and the spending date. Test whether another authorized adult can operate the system for thirty days.

Build a protected financial emergency file containing key identification, accounts, obligations, insurance, tax, medical and legal records plus verified contacts. Quarterly reviews should produce dated changes rather than another list of intentions.

Create a property inventory and test retrieval of emergency records. Preparedness requires both secure access and a backup when the primary device or home is unavailable. Keep legal, tax and insurance questions with the qualified professional responsible for them.

Update retirement and insurance beneficiaries separately from wills. Confirm primary and contingent choices, percentages, legal names and contact information. Confirm every automated transfer after the first execution rather than assuming setup succeeded.

Review wills, powers of attorney, health directives, guardianship choices and titles with qualified local professionals, including applicable signing and storage requirements. Preserve statements and calculations so next year starts with evidence instead of memory.

Finish with a one-page dashboard assigning every transfer, form, review and record update to a person and date. A plan becomes useful only when it can execute. An annual plan is successful when ordinary decisions become easier and shocks remain survivable.

faq.question: Should the twelve moves follow calendar months?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Sequence them by urgency, deadlines and dependencies. Cash flow and protection gaps usually come before optional optimization.

faq.question: How often should I review the plan?
faq.answer: Review upcoming cash flow every payday, the dashboard quarterly and the complete plan after major income, family, housing or health changes.

faq.question: Should debt payoff come before emergency savings?
faq.answer: Coordinate them. Maintain required payments, build a starter reserve and direct additional cash according to debt cost and household risk.

faq.question: Where should annual expenses be saved?
faq.answer: Use clearly labelled sinking funds in an appropriate stable account, separate in the ledger from emergency and long-term investment money.

faq.question: Do I need to change investments every year?
faq.answer: No. Review allocation, fees and goals, but trade only when the portfolio or facts justify it under the written plan.

faq.question: Is updating a will enough to update beneficiaries?
faq.answer: Not always. Retirement and insurance designations can control assets separately, so review each account and coordinate with legal advice.

faq.question: What makes an annual plan complete?
faq.answer: Each action has a current fact base, amount or document, responsible person, deadline and follow-up verification.

glossary.definition: Dated view of income, transfers and obligations rather than monthly totals alone.
Money accumulated gradually for a known future expense.
First reserve layer intended to absorb a likely urgent shock.
Standardized yearly borrowing cost including interest and specified fees.
Tax payment taken from income and credited toward final liability.
Distribution of investments among categories with different risk characteristics.
Restoring investments toward the intended allocation.
First person or entity designated to receive an account or policy benefit.
Backup recipient if a primary beneficiary cannot receive the benefit.
Legal authority for an agent to act within powers granted by a valid document.
